parts.article:
Petrol power: an eco-revolution?
 
A Laura Ingalls Wilder's semi-autobiographical novel The Long Winter describes how the inhabitants of a small town called De Smet in the American Midwest narrowly avoided starvation during the severe winter of 1880–1881. Over three metres of snow fell on the northern plains, immobilising the railways and cutting off the settlers from the rest of the world. Laura and her neighbours were only saved when her fiancé and his friend trudged 30 kilometres through the snow to fetch food, risking their lives in the process. The story is a reminder of how lethal geographical isolation and crop failures could be before the advent of modern farming and transportation technologies. Not long ago, subsistence farmers in many countries had to cope with the 'lean season' – the period of greatest scarcity before new crops became available. In England, late spring was once referred to as the 'hungry gap'. The situation was made worse by the cost of moving heavy things over muddy dirt roads; three centuries ago, moving goods 50 kilometres on land between, say, Liverpool and Manchester was as expensive as shipping them across the North Atlantic.
 
B The development of coal-powered railways and steamships in the 19th century revolutionized the lives of farmers. Instead of having to grow everything they needed, they could now specialise in what they did best and rely on other producers for their remaining needs. The result was not only food and ever-cheaper prices, but the end of widespread famine and starvation, as the surplus from regions with good harvests could now be transported to those that had experienced mediocre ones. Since then, petroleum-derived fuels have largely displaced coal because of their higher energy density, cleaner combustion and greater ease of extraction, further improving road and rail transportation systems.
 
C While the convenience of modern methods of transportation is obvious, few people grasp their historical significance in terms of their beneficial impact on large cities and the health of residents. In 1898, delegates gathered in New York City for the world's first international urban-planning conference. The topic that dominated discussions was not infrastructure or housing, but horse manure. The problem was that as the populations of cities like New York and London grew, the number of horses there also grew, and in New York these produced nearly two million kilograms of manure each day. If this problem continued, it was estimated that by 1950 every street in London would be buried three metres deep in horse manure. Unable to think of any solution, the delegates concluded that urban living was inherently unsustainable.
 
D Paradoxically, much of the urban manure problem was related to the growth of the railways. The ability to deliver perishable goods, such as meat and dairy products, from locations that benefited from better soil and climate, put many farms located near cities out of business. As these had relied on manure from city workhorses for fertiliser, the demand for this was greatly reduced. The impact of urban workhorses was felt both in the cities and in the countryside. In cities, apart from their overpowering stench, the manure piles were prime breeding grounds for house flies, perhaps three billion of which hatched each day in US cities in the early 20th century. With flies came outbreaks of typhoid, cholera and diphtheria. Workhorses sometimes panicked in heavy traffic and kicked or bit bystanders. The clatter of wagon wheels on cobblestone pavement could be deafening, and since a horse and wagon occupied more street space than a modern truck, they also created significant traffic congestion, while a horse that collapsed on the road created an obstruction that was difficult to remove. The countryside also suffered. To supply the workhorses with oats and hay, additional land had to be cleared of its natural animal life and vegetation, and sometimes water had to be diverted to irrigate it, with considerable negative effects on the whole area.
 
E So, while the trains, cars and trucks of the early 20th century were noisy and polluting by today's standards, they were regarded as a significant improvement on what had gone before. Before they were available, poor soils often meant that a large amount of land was required to sustain a household, and much environmental damage, primarily in the form of soil erosion, was caused by trying to farm these soils. It could be argued that modern transportation allowed the development of remote regions like the Canadian Prairies and allowed more suitable crops to be grown in the poorer soils in Europe before being sold elsewhere.
 
F Over time, the concentration of food production in the world's best locations allowed some agricultural land to revert to a wild state. For instance, France benefited from an expansion of its forest area by one third between 1830 and 1960. This so-called 'forest transition' occurred in the context of a doubling of the French population and a dramatic increase in standards of living. Improvements in logistics also allowed the production and export of food from locations where water was abundant to regions where it was scarce, thus preventing the depletion of water resources there. It also made possible a drastic increase in the size of our cities. Contrary to what most people believe, the growth in cities is a positive development. In the words of economist Ed Glaeser: 'Residing in a forest might seem to be a good way of showing one's love of nature, but living in a concrete jungle is actually far more ecologically friendly... If you love nature, stay away from it.' It could be argued that modern transportation technologies have been a major contributor to a wealthier, cleaner and more sustainable world.
parts.questions:
Questions 27–30
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 27–30 on your answer sheet.

Q27 Why were the inhabitants of De Smet in danger of starvation?

  • A The trains were unable to operate normally.
  • B The harvest had been completely destroyed.
  • C The roads to the town had not yet been built.
  • D The farmers were reluctant to sell their produce.

Q28 What problem did subsistence farmers have in the past?

  • A They had no effective means of storing food.
  • B Food was expensive because of high shipping costs.
  • C Their access to food was limited at certain times.
  • D Food could not be transported for long distances by road.

Q29 The writer says that the use of coal to power railways and steamships

  • A led to a greater range of fresh vegetables being available in urban areas.
  • B was less efficient than the use of petroleum-derived products.
  • C allowed farmers to be more self-sufficient than they were previously.
  • D was better for the environment than using petroleum-derived products.

Q30 The writer refers to an urban-planning conference held in 1898 in order to

  • A illustrate a problem that was later solved by modern technology.
  • B give an example of poor decisions made about urban planning.
  • C show that urban issues were misunderstood in the past.
  • D indicate the disregard at the time for public health concerns.
Questions 31–35
Complete the summary using the list of words, A-J, below.
Write the correct letter, A-J, in boxes 31–35 on your answer sheet.
Problems caused by urban workhorses

In cities, the large amounts of horse manure led to in the streets and were also linked to the spread of . In certain situations, the horses might even cause to passers-by. There were also the problems of noise and congestion caused by horse-drawn vehicles. In the countryside, there were problems too. The was damaged because of the need to provide for urban workhorses.

  • A rich landowners
  • B injuries
  • C food
  • D accidental falls
  • E environment
  • F dangerous area
  • G use of irrigation
  • H unpleasant smells
  • I treatment
  • J diseases
Questions 36–40
Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 36–40 on your answer sheet, write:

Q36 Farmers whose land was poor failed to benefit from modern forms of transport.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q37 Between 1830 and 1960 there were positive effects associated with changing patterns of agriculture in France.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q38 A fairer distribution of the world's water resources is needed.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q39 Living in the countryside does less harm to the environment than living in a city.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q40 It is possible that modern developments in transportation have had a beneficial impact on the world.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

reference:
Q27

干扰 B（收成被毁）文中未提及；C（路未修好）文中说的是雪封路，而非未建；D（农民不愿卖）文中未提及。

句子 (Paragraph A) “Over three metres of snow fell... immobilising the railways and cutting off the settlers...”

解析 题目问为什么De Smet的居民面临饥饿的危险。原文A段提到“immobilising the railways（使铁路瘫痪）”和“cutting off the settlers（切断了定居者与外界的联系）”，导致食物无法运入，对应选项 A (The trains were unable to operate normally)。

Q28

解析 题目问过去的自给自足农民面临什么问题。原文A段提到他们必须应对“lean season（青黄不接的时期/贫瘠季节）”，这是“greatest scarcity before new crops became available（新庄稼收获前极度匮乏的时期）”，对应选项 C (Their access to food was limited at certain times)。

干扰 A（无法储存）未提及；B（运费高）是针对货物运输，不是自给农民的核心痛点；D（无法长途运输）原文说的是贵，不是不能。

句子 (Paragraph A) “...subsistence farmers... had to cope with the 'lean season' – the period of greatest scarcity...”

Q29

解析 题目问作者关于使用煤炭驱动铁路和轮船说了什么。原文B段提到石油衍生燃料取代了煤炭，因为石油具有“higher energy density, cleaner combustion（更高的能量密度，更清洁的燃烧）”，反过来说明煤炭效率较低，对应选项 B (was less efficient than the use of petroleum-derived products)。

干扰 这是一个比较级逻辑推断。石油比煤炭好 = 煤炭不如石油高效。

句子 (Paragraph B) “...petroleum-derived fuels have largely displaced coal because of their higher energy density...”

Q30

句子 (Paragraph C) “The topic that dominated discussions was... horse manure... Unable to think of any solution...” (Combined with Title/Theme).

解析 题目问作者提到1898年城市规划会议是为了什么。原文C段提到会议讨论的主导话题是“horse manure（马粪）”，当时认为城市生活“inherently unsustainable（本质上不可持续）”。但后文（D段、E段）指出随着火车、汽车（modern technology）的出现，马被取代了，问题解决了。因此引用该会议是为了说明一个后来被现代技术解决的问题，对应选项 A。

干扰 作者引用历史困境是为了引出下文的“石油动力革命（eco-revolution）”作为解决方案。

Q31

解析 题目说在城市里，大量马粪导致街道上的____。原文D段提到马粪堆除了“overpowering stench（强烈的恶臭）”外，还是苍蝇的滋生地。Stench对应选项 H (unpleasant smells)。

干扰 “Stench” 对应 “unpleasant smells”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “In cities, apart from their overpowering stench...”

Q32

解析 题目说马粪还与____的传播有关。原文D段提到随着苍蝇而来的是“outbreaks of typhoid, cholera and diphtheria（伤寒、霍乱和白喉的爆发）”，这些都是疾病，对应选项 J (diseases)。

干扰 具体疾病名称概括为 “diseases”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “With flies came outbreaks of typhoid, cholera and diphtheria.”

Q33

解析 题目说在某些情况下，马甚至可能对路人造成____。原文D段提到工作马有时会恐慌并“kicked or bit bystanders（踢或咬旁观者）”，这会导致伤害，对应选项 B (injuries)。

干扰 “Kicked or bit” 导致的结果是 “injuries”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “Workhorses sometimes... kicked or bit bystanders.”

Q34

干扰 “Natural animal life and vegetation / whole area” 对应 “environment”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “...with considerable negative effects on the whole area.”

解析 题目说在农村，____受到了破坏。原文D段末尾提到为了供应马匹，额外的土地不得不被清理，水被改道，对“whole area（整个区域）”造成了相当大的负面影响。结合上下文语境（land cleared, natural animal life），受损的是环境，对应选项 E (environment)。

Q35

解析 题目说这是因为需要为城市工作马提供____。原文D段提到为了供应工作马“oats and hay（燕麦和干草）”，这些是马的食物，对应选项 C (food)。

干扰 “Oats and hay” 是马的 “food”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “To supply the workhorses with oats and hay...”

Q36

解析 题目说土地贫瘠的农民未能（failed to）从现代交通方式中受益。原文E段末尾提到现代交通允许“suitable crops to be grown in the poorer soils... before being sold elsewhere（在贫瘠土壤种植合适的作物……然后销往别处）”。能把作物卖出去就是受益（benefit），题目与原文矛盾，选 NO。

干扰 原文说 “allowed... to be grown... sold”，即带来了商业机会，反驳了 “failed to benefit”。

句子 (Paragraph E) “...allowed more suitable crops to be grown in the poorer soils in Europe before being sold elsewhere.”

Q37

句子 (Paragraph F) “France benefited from an expansion of its forest area... dramatic increase in standards of living.”

解析 题目说1830年至1960年间，法国农业模式的变化带来了积极影响（positive effects）。原文F段提到法国“benefited from an expansion of its forest area（受益于森林面积的扩大）”，且这发生在生活水平显著提高的背景下，选 YES。

干扰 “Benefited / increase in standards of living” 对应 “positive effects”。

Q38

解析 题目说世界水资源需要更公平的分配（fairer distribution）。原文F段只提到物流改善允许从水资源丰富地区生产食物出口到稀缺地区，从而“preventing the depletion（防止枯竭）”。文中陈述了食物贸易对水资源压力的缓解作用，但未提出“需要重新分配水资源本身”或提及“公平性（fairer）”的呼吁，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 原文讲的是通过运粮（虚拟水）来解决问题，没提分配水资源（distribution of water resources）的公平性主张。

句子 (Paragraph F) “...export of food from locations where water was abundant to regions where it was scarce...”

Q39

解析 题目说住在农村比住在城市对环境的危害更小（less harm）。原文F段引用经济学家Ed Glaeser的话：“living in a concrete jungle [city] is actually far more ecologically friendly（住在水泥丛林[城市]实际上对生态更友好）”，即住在城市危害更小，住在农村（residing in a forest）反而不好。题目说反了，选 NO。

干扰 “City is more ecologically friendly” 反驳了 “Countryside does less harm”。

句子 (Paragraph F) “...living in a concrete jungle is actually far more ecologically friendly...”

Q40

解析 题目说现代交通发展可能（It is possible）对世界产生了有益影响。原文F段最后一句：“It could be argued that modern transportation technologies have been a major contributor to a wealthier, cleaner and more sustainable world（可以认为现代交通技术是创造更富裕、更清洁、更可持续世界的主要贡献者）”，选 YES。

干扰 “Could be argued” 对应 “It is possible”，“Contributor to a... sustainable world” 对应 “beneficial impact”。

句子 (Paragraph F) “It could be argued that modern transportation technologies have been a major contributor to a wealthier, cleaner and more sustainable world.”
